subtopics.title: Reading the Table Before You Draw

questions.question: In the schedule, quantity demanded falls from 250 to 50 as price climbs. This column will become:
options: A downward-sloping demand curve
An upward-sloping demand curve
A horizontal line
The supply curve

questions.question: The supply column grows from 50 to 250 as price rises because:
options: Sellers make mistakes at low prices
The law of supply — higher prices draw larger quantities onto the market
The law of demand applies to sellers
The table was printed upside down

questions.question: Why does the row at fifteen rand deserve special attention?
options: It has the highest quantities
It is the cheapest price
Both columns read 150 — the curves will cross exactly there
It is the middle of the page

subtopics.title: Axes, Scales and Plotting the Points

questions.question: The standing convention for economics graphs places:
options: Price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Quantity on the vertical axis and price on the horizontal axis
Both variables on the same axis
Time on the horizontal axis

questions.question: Why must the scale use equal steps along each axis?
options: It looks tidier for the marker
Uneven steps warp the curves and corrupt every reading taken from the graph
Equal steps save paper
The steps must match the other axis exactly

questions.question: Plotting the row "ten rand, demand 200" means:
options: Up to 200 on the price axis, across to ten
Up to ten on the price axis, across to 200, mark the point
A point anywhere between the axes
Drawing a vertical line at ten

questions.question: Which of these belongs on a complete market graph?
options: Only the two curves
Curves and a title, but no axis labels
Axis labels, a heading, and D and S written on the curves
A key explaining the colour of the paper

questions.question: On our graph the curves cross at:
options: Price fifteen rand, quantity 150 — the market equilibrium
Price twenty rand, quantity 100
Price five rand, quantity 250
They never cross

questions.question: If your curves cross at a price where the table's two columns are NOT equal:
options: The table must be wrong
A point is plotted incorrectly — check each point against its row
The market has two equilibria
Nothing needs checking

questions.question: The dotted lines from the crossing to the two axes:
options: Are decoration and can be left out
Show the shaded surplus region
Demonstrate the reading of equilibrium price and quantity, and often carry marks
Represent a second demand curve

subtopics.title: Reading Off Excess Supply at R20

questions.question: At twenty rand, the horizontal sweep reads demand 100 and supply 200. The excess supply is:
options: 100 units — quantity supplied minus quantity demanded at that one price
300 units — the two quantities added
200 units — the supply reading alone
50 units — the smallest number in the table

questions.question: Why does a surplus appear at twenty rand specifically?
options: Because twenty is an even number
Because twenty rand lies above the equilibrium price of fifteen — sellers are drawn in while buyers are priced out
Because demand shifted left at twenty
Because the table ends at twenty-five

questions.question: Asked for the excess demand at ten rand, you would find:
options: A surplus of 100 units
Zero — ten rand is the equilibrium
A shortage of 100 units — demand 200 against supply 100
A shortage of 250 units

questions.question: The most frequent error in gap-reading questions is:
options: Using dotted lines
Subtracting the smaller number from the larger
Labelling the gap
Reading the two curves at different prices instead of one height touching both

questions.question: "The table is the boss" means:
options: Every point on the graph comes from a table row — when they disagree, the table wins
Tables are harder than graphs
The graph can improve on the table's numbers
Only tables appear in assessments

questions.question: Interviewing the columns BEFORE drawing helps because:
options: It uses up spare time
Knowing the picture must run downhill and uphill lets you catch your own plotting mistakes
The columns change once drawn
It replaces the need to plot at all

questions.question: The "handshake row" at fifteen rand is special because:
options: It has the largest quantities
Sellers refuse to trade there
Both columns agree at 150 — the one price where buyers' and sellers' plans match, where the curves must cross
It is the first row of the table

questions.question: The three framing habits are:
options: Price up the side and quantity along the bottom; even steps; name everything
Use colour; draw fast; skip labels
Big axes; small dots; thick lines
Title first; curves second; axes last

questions.question: An uneven scale is compared to a measuring tape with squashed centimetres because:
options: Both are cheaper to make
Whatever it tells you afterwards is worthless — the distortion poisons every reading
Both stretch when wet
Neither affects the answer

questions.question: Plotting as "deliveries" means:
options: Drawing the curve first and adding dots later
Guessing where the line should bend
Each row gives coordinates — ride up to the price, across to the quantity, leave a dot
Delivering the graph to the front of the class

questions.question: If every dot lands at its correct coordinates:
options: The curves still need to be forced into shape
The demand line may slope either way
The graph must be redrawn to check
The downhill and uphill lines appear on their own — the two laws draw themselves

questions.question: Feeding the machine "twenty rand" returns:
options: Demand 100, supply 200 — an excess supply of 100 units visible as the gap between the lines
Demand 200, supply 100 — a shortage
Equilibrium at twenty rand
No reading at all

questions.question: The level sweep at ten rand shows buyers overshooting sellers by 100 units. This is called:
options: Excess supply
Excess demand — a shortage at a price below the resting place
Market failure
A shift of demand

questions.question: The one sweeping rule that keeps every reading honest is:
options: Always start from the quantity axis
Read the higher curve first
BOTH touches on ONE height — never read the two curves at different prices
Use a red pen for surpluses

questions.question: The lesson calls this skill routine rather than talent because:
options: Only talented learners can draw graphs
Routines cannot be learned
Graphs are optional in this subject
Interview, frame, deliver, sweep — repeatable steps that five practice graphs make permanent
